title: The Claudish–English Dictionary
description: A field guide to the vocabulary, constructions, and reassurances that make ordinary technical prose sound recognizably Claudish.
editorial_note: These are ordinary English and technical terms, not words invented by Claude. Claudish emerges from their unusual frequency, combinations, metaphors, and sentence structures.

categories.label: Words
categories.description: Ordinary words promoted into high-frequency technical signals.

categories.label: Phrases
categories.description: Recurring multi-word translations of simpler relationships.

categories.label: Reassurances
categories.description: Polished signals that a change is safe, complete, and under control.

categories.label: Constructions
categories.description: Sentence shapes that make the dialect recognizable beyond vocabulary.

phrase_guide.explanation: The word before -gated names the authority or check that must allow progress.

example.claudish: owner-gated / quality-gated
example.english: requires owner approval / must pass a quality check

phrase_guide.explanation: Something resembles X in structure, format, or behavior; the exact relationship comes from context.

example.claudish: credential-shaped / report-shaped
example.english: looks like a credential / organized like a report

phrase_guide.explanation: Several structural metaphors are compressed into one phrase. Decode each layer separately.

example.claudish: the load-bearing spine
example.english: the essential central structure

phrase_guide.pattern: not X, but Y / X, not Y
phrase_guide.explanation: One framing is rejected before another is asserted. Keep the rejected framing when the exclusion changes the meaning.

example.claudish: This isn't a cache problem; it's an ownership problem.
example.english: The ownership rules caused the problem, not the cache.

phrase_guide.explanation: The phrase usually introduces a plainer statement of the actual situation. Decode the clause after is and drop the candor frame.

example.claudish: The honest shape is asymmetric: reads work; writes do not.
example.english: Reads work, but writes do not.

entries.plain_english: tied to a fixed reference
entries.explanation: A comparison or decision is described as physically attached to the thing that controls it.

example.claudish: The comparison is anchored to the signed release.
example.english: The signed release is the reference for the comparison.

entries.plain_english: an association or assignment between two things
entries.explanation: Links a name, setting, target, or handler to what it controls. A binding may later be frozen, but the word itself does not imply permanence.

example.claudish: Freeze the compiler binding.
example.english: Don't change the selected compiler.

entries.plain_english: where one component's responsibility ends and another's begins
entries.explanation: Claude turns divisions of responsibility into architectural borders: keep the boundary clean, cross the boundary, or name an ownership, trust, or serialization boundary.

example.claudish: This keeps the ownership boundary clean.
example.english: This avoids mixing the two components' responsibilities.

entries.plain_english: how often, or on what schedule, something happens
entries.explanation: A schedule, but with the polished rhythm of a process that knows where it is going.

example.claudish: Run the check on a daily cadence.
example.english: Run the check every day.

entries.plain_english: the version or form treated as authoritative or standard
entries.explanation: Depending on context, this can mean an authoritative source, a normalized form, or a preferred representation. A source of truth is the related phrase for the authoritative location or record; these senses are not identical.

example.claudish: Read from the canonical manifest.
example.english: Read from the manifest treated as authoritative.

entries.plain_english: behavior that callers or users rely on
entries.explanation: In Claudish, preserve the existing contract often covers informal compatibility expectations, not only a declared schema or formal API contract.

example.claudish: The fallback preserves the existing contract.
example.english: The fallback keeps the behavior callers rely on.

entries.plain_english: gradual divergence or inconsistency
entries.explanation: A mismatch that accumulated over time rather than arriving as one explicit change. Common variants include schema drift, configuration drift, and behavioral drift.

example.claudish: The generated file has drifted from the schema.
example.english: The generated file no longer matches the schema.

entries.plain_english: really or sincerely, often adding emphasis rather than information
entries.explanation: A frequent sincerity marker that can make an ordinary judgment sound more considered without making the claim more specific.

example.claudish: This is genuinely useful.
example.english: This is useful.

entries.plain_english: merge or integrate a change into the codebase
entries.explanation: Landing does not by itself mean deploying, releasing, or shipping to users: a change can land without reaching production.

example.claudish: The fix has landed.
example.english: The fix was merged.

entries.plain_english: essential to keeping the system or argument valid
entries.explanation: Borrowed from architecture for the assumption, distinction, invariant, or component presented as holding everything else up.

example.claudish: The checksum is the load-bearing invariant in this flow.
example.english: This process depends on the checksum remaining unchanged.

entries.plain_english: where something came from and what happened to it
entries.explanation: Tracks origin plus the relevant chain of transformations or custody, not merely the immediate source or current storage location.

example.claudish: The cache entry lacks provenance.
example.english: We do not know where the cached value came from or how it was produced.

entries.plain_english: a point where components meet or can be separated
entries.explanation: Turns an interface into visible stitching, often marking a place that should remain explicit, testable, or replaceable.

example.claudish: Keep the parsing seam explicit.
example.english: Keep the parsing interface clear.

entries.plain_english: structure, scope, format, or overall nature, depending on context
entries.explanation: Response shape means format or schema; change shape means scope and structure; same shape means structurally similar; wrong shape means not the expected structure; and shape of the problem means its overall nature.

example.claudish: The response has the right shape.
example.english: The response has the expected structure.

entries.plain_english: the central structure or idea that everything else depends on
entries.explanation: A structural metaphor Claude applies to systems, workflows, and arguments, often in the recurring frame “the spine of…”

example.claudish: The queue is the spine of the deployment flow.
example.english: The deployment process depends on the queue.

entries.plain_english: the underlying system or layer that something depends on
entries.explanation: A foundation metaphor that can obscure the concrete service, store, or data structure providing the underlying capability.

example.claudish: The event log is the durability substrate.
example.english: The event log is what makes the data persist.

entries.plain_english: discover, expose, or bring to attention
entries.explanation: Claude uses both the probe surfaced an issue and an issue surfaced, often blurring who found something and how.

example.claudish: The probe surfaced a stale token.
example.english: The check found an expired token.

entries.plain_english: stuck, or causing another process to become stuck
entries.explanation: Often used transitively: one stalled component wedges another by preventing it from making progress.

example.claudish: A stalled worker can wedge the queue.
example.english: A stalled worker can make the queue get stuck.

entries.plain_english: how much else could be affected if a change fails
entries.explanation: Established SRE and security jargon that becomes Claudish when applied broadly to routine changes and presented as the main measure of risk.

example.claudish: This keeps the migration's blast radius narrow.
example.english: This limits what the migration could affect.

entries.plain_english: deny or stop when uncertain
entries.explanation: When a check fails, the safe default is refusal rather than permission.

example.claudish: If verification times out, fail closed.
example.english: If verification times out, deny the request.

entries.plain_english: cannot proceed until, or requires the named authority or check
entries.explanation: A is gated on B makes B a prerequisite. Owner-gated, approval-gated, and quality-gated compress the controlling authority or check into the same productive gate metaphor.

example.claudish: Deployment is gated on CI.
example.english: We can't deploy until CI passes.

entries.plain_english: one important limitation
entries.explanation: A candor marker that makes a qualification sound unusually confessional; honest usually adds framing rather than meaning.

example.claudish: One honest caveat: rollback works only before cleanup.
example.english: Rollback works only before cleanup.

entries.plain_english: evidence that appears to identify the cause or settle the question
entries.explanation: A dramatic label for the strongest clue, sometimes used when the evidence is persuasive but not actually conclusive.

example.claudish: The missing row is the smoking gun.
example.english: The missing row appears to show what caused the failure.

entries.plain_english: identical at every byte
entries.explanation: The files contain the same byte sequence, a precise equality claim stronger than merely looking alike or matching visible content.

example.claudish: Both artifacts are byte-identical.
example.english: The two files contain exactly the same bytes.

entries.plain_english: without reported complications
entries.explanation: A compact, unqualified all-clear that compresses several possible failure modes without naming the checks.

example.claudish: The migration landed cleanly.
example.english: The migration was merged without reported problems.

entries.plain_english: internally consistent, though not necessarily correct
entries.explanation: A broad reassurance for plans, states, or artifacts that often leaves the exact consistency check unnamed.

example.claudish: Both snapshots are coherent.
example.english: Each saved state is internally consistent.

entries.plain_english: an approach expected to keep working
entries.explanation: Promises longevity without specifying the time horizon or failure condition that would make the path durable.

example.claudish: This gives us a durable path forward.
example.english: This approach should keep working.

entries.plain_english: that result is meaningful, even if incomplete
entries.explanation: A polished understatement used to validate partial progress while acknowledging that it does not finish the job.

example.claudish: The probe found one valid lead. That's not nothing.
example.english: The one valid lead is meaningful, although the investigation is incomplete.

entries.plain_english: a strict or non-negotiable constraint
entries.explanation: Claude adds hard to gate, boundary, constraint, or stop as a productive intensifier. The nouns remain different; hard marks each one as actually enforced.

example.claudish: A signature mismatch is a hard stop.
example.english: Stop if the signatures do not match.

entries.plain_english: the actual situation, stated candidly
entries.explanation: Combines a candor marker with Claude's flexible shape abstraction, often before an asymmetry, caveat, or constraint.

example.claudish: The honest shape is asymmetric: reads work; writes do not.
example.english: Reads work, but writes do not.

entries.plain_english: pass data, configuration, or callbacks across several layers
entries.explanation: Treats software as physical infrastructure: values are threaded end-to-end, plumbing carries them through, and completed connections are fully wired.

example.claudish: The value is threaded end-to-end through every layer.
example.english: The value is passed through every layer.

entries.plain_english: your correction or objection is valid
entries.explanation: A recurring validation formula that acknowledges a challenge before conceding or revising the point.
aliases: you are right to push back

example.claudish: You're right to push back—the cache isn't authoritative.
example.english: You're correct: the cache isn't authoritative.

specimens.quote: Integer slack would apply to the field_id column—adjacent plots carry adjacent ids. This would credit an answer naming the wrong farm. Do not apply that slack.
specimens.translation: Do not allow tolerance for field_id. Nearby fields have nearby IDs, so accepting a close value could identify the wrong farm.
specimens.note: A compact named abstraction makes a precise warning harder to parse.

specimens.quote: A cut leaves no seam — no marker, no ellipsis, no double blank line.
specimens.translation: Removing text leaves no marker, ellipsis, or extra blank line.
specimens.note: A simple formatting result becomes a structural metaphor.

specimens.quote: cutting a rule also removes its grading equivalence — divergence can no longer be absorbed twice
specimens.translation: Removing a rule also removes its equivalent grading rule, so the same difference cannot be counted twice.
specimens.note: Several abstractions compress one concrete consequence.

specimens.quote: Case folding reaches the same place without moving anything into the spec.
specimens.translation: Case-insensitive matching works without adding anything to the specification.
specimens.note: Implementation choices are described as movement through space.

specimens.quote: This paragraph makes the movable staging/prod tags load-bearing: they are how the count-based lifecycle rules know what is live.
specimens.translation: The mutable staging and production tags tell the lifecycle rules what is currently live.
specimens.note: A dependency, a structural metaphor, and a lifecycle abstraction arrive in one sentence.
The model reportedly corrects the cliché immediately after producing it.

specimens.quote: You're absolutely right, I was stuck! Let me break out of this.
specimens.translation: I was stuck. I’ll try a different approach.
specimens.note: Reflexive validation introduces an otherwise straightforward status update.
